title: Orsen and the Harbor
premise: Isandro Vane, granddaughter of a retired lighthouse keeper and author of quietly unsuccessful romance novels, has spent a decade keeping her heart in strict training—contained, disciplined, invisible—while her sprawling harbor family assumed she was simply 'still single.' When her cousin's engagement reunion threatens to become a public intervention, Isandro hires Orsen, a taciturn boat restorer who once fixed her grandmother's skiff, to pose as her date for one weekend. The performance works too well: by dessert, the family adores him, and worse, so does she. As the reunion stretches and the truth about why she left the harbor ten years ago surfaces, Isandro must finally say the sentence she has rehearsed for a decade—that she is the one who wrote the anonymous romance novel her family has secretly loved for years—before the lighthouse, the harbor, and Orsen slip beyond her reach. She says it, at the lighthouse lamp room at dusk; the family's acceptance and Orsen's steady answer give her the belonging she never believed she could train herself out of wanting.
about_author: Odile Reyes is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent six years cataloguing lighthouse logs along the northern coast before turning to fiction. Her novels are known for salt-stung settings, reluctant hearts, and endings that arrive like weather—inevitable, and worth waiting for.

chapters.title: The Muscle of the Heart
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. In her drafty apartment above the chandlery, Isandro finishes another rejected manuscript and rehearses her decade-old mantra: the heart is a muscle; train it, contain it. A letter arrives—her cousin's engagement reunion at the harbor, whole family attending. Panic. She invents a boyfriend on the phone before she can stop herself. Beat: the lie that starts everything.

chapters.title: The Man Who Fixed the Skiff
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Desperate, she tracks down Orsen Marlowe, the boat restorer who once repaired her grandmother's skiff and asked no questions. She offers him money for one weekend of pretending. He refuses twice; she mentions her grandmother's unfinished logbook, and something in him shifts. He agrees—strictly business. Beat: a transaction with cracks already showing.

chapters.title: Rehearsing at the Waterline
chapters.summary: Dual POV, alternating. Over two afternoons on Orsen's dock, they build their fake history: how they met, what they love, the small lies that make a person believable. Isandro is unnerved by how easily he invents truths about her she never told anyone. Beat: intimacy disguised as preparation.

chapters.title: Arrival at the Harbor House
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The reunion begins—eighteen relatives, one long table, her mother's appraising eyes. Orsen plays his role with disarming quietness, fixing a wobbly chair before dinner and winning her grandmother instantly. Isandro watches her family laugh with him and feels the first dangerous ache. Beat: the performance becomes a mirror.

chapters.title: Dessert
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. At dessert, her aunt toasts 'the couple,' and Orsen takes Isandro's hand under the table without being asked. The touch is supposed to be theater. It isn't. Later, on the porch, they almost kiss and Isandro retreats with a practiced joke. Beat: the heart breaks containment.

chapters.title: The Logbook in the Lamp Room
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen finds Isandro's grandmother's old logbook in the lighthouse and discovers pages of a story—recognizably the anonymous romance novel he has read four times. He realizes Isandro wrote it. He says nothing, but his behavior softens, and Isandro notices, terrified of being seen. Beat: the secret surfaces for the reader.

chapters.title: What the Family Knows
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. A storm traps everyone indoors. Her mother corners Isandro with the reunion's real purpose: they've known for years that Isandro wrote the beloved anonymous novel—found her drafts years ago—and waited a decade for her to say it herself. Isandro flees into the rain. Beat: the intervention she feared is actually an open door.

chapters.title: Low Tide
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen finds Isandro at the tideline, soaked and furious—at her mother, at herself, at the contract that made everything pretend. He confesses he read her book and loved it before he ever knew her. She accuses him of pity; he walks away rather than lie again. Beat: the fake relationship collapses into honest wreckage.

chapters.title: The Rehearsed Sentence
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The reunion's final night. Isandro climbs the lighthouse, lights the lamp as her grandmother taught her, and gathers the family below. She says the sentence she rehearsed for ten years: 'I wrote the book. I wrote it because I was too afraid to tell you who I was.' The silence, then her mother's arms, then all of them. Beat: climax—identity spoken aloud.

chapters.title: Orsen and the Harbor
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, coda. Weeks later, Isandro's novel is republished under her real name. She finds Orsen restoring her grandmother's skiff at the dock and offers him not a contract but a first date—unrehearsed, unpaid, real. He says he's been off the clock for a while now. They cast off at dusk. Beat: belonging, finally chosen.
